question: Q3
claim: A microbial transglutaminase from Kutzneria albida (KalbTG) enables highly site-specific protein labeling with no cross-reactivity to standard mTG substrates or common target proteins such as antibodies.
evidence: KalbTG showed no cross-reactivity with known mTG substrates; fusing its recognition motif to a target allows site-specific, ratio-controlled conjugation with low label excess, enabling orthogonal enzymatic crosslinking.

sources.title: Discovery of a microbial transglutaminase enabling highly site-specific labeling of proteins

verification.note: Demonstrated site-specificity in vitro for bioconjugation; not yet applied to a clinical sealant.

question: Q3
claim: Active, soluble recombinant mTG can be produced directly in the E. coli cytosol by engineering the propeptide of the zymogen (e.g. K10R/Y12A substitutions) without external protease activation.
evidence: A soluble K10R/Y12A pro-mTG mutant expressed in E. coli cytosol retained intramolecular-chaperone folding while relieving active-site inhibition, yielding substrate-dependent activity.

sources.title: Engineered Active Zymogen of Microbial Transglutaminase (bioRxiv)
Engineering the Propeptide of Microbial Transglutaminase Zymogen (Bioconjugate Chemistry)

verification.note: Demonstrated recombinant expression; still proof-of-concept for bioconjugation, not sealant manufacturing.

question: Q3
claim: Self-cleavable zymogen constructs (TEV protease fused to pro-mTG with K9R/Y11A propeptide mutations) allow recombinant production of active soluble mTG in E. coli.
evidence: A chimeric TEV-protease/mTG-zymogen with K9R and Y11A propeptide mutations self-cleaves, dissociates the propeptide, and yields active soluble enzyme.

sources.title: Recombinant production of active microbial transglutaminase in E. coli by using self-cleavable zymogen with mutated propeptide

verification.note: Demonstrated production route; laboratory scale.

question: Q3
claim: Directed evolution has produced mTG variants with substantially improved activity and thermostability, e.g. the E164L single mutant.
evidence: Error-prone PCR yielded E164L, which showed ~1.95x specific activity of wild-type at 50 C and a 1.66-fold longer half-life at 50 C.

sources.title: Enhancing the activity and thermostability of Streptomyces mobaraensis transglutaminase by directed evolution and molecular dynamics simulation

verification.note: Demonstrated quantitative improvement in vitro.

question: Q3
claim: Multi-site engineered mTG variants (penta-mutants) and the S2P variant achieve markedly higher thermostability than wild-type.
evidence: Combining thermostabilizing mutations into penta-site variants and an N-terminal Ser2->Pro (S2P) exchange produced remarkably increased thermostability at 60 C after one mutagenesis round.

sources.title: Random mutagenesis of a recombinant microbial transglutaminase for the generation of thermostable and heat-sensitive variants
Active secretion of a thermostable transglutaminase variant in Escherichia coli

verification.note: Demonstrated thermostability gains across multiple independent studies.

question: Q3
claim: Wild-type microbial transglutaminase is immunogenic in humans and generates neo-epitope antibodies, motivating low-immunogenicity engineered variants for implantable use.
evidence: mTG-treated gluten/food proteins induced antibodies in humans and neo-epitope mTG antibodies appear in systemic circulation; mTG is implicated as a potential inducer in celiac disease and autoimmunity, contradicting non-immunogenic claims.

sources.title: Microbial Transglutaminase Is Immunogenic and Potentially Pathogenic in Pediatric Celiac Disease
Processed Food Additive Microbial Transglutaminase and Its Cross-Linked Gliadin Complexes Are Potential Public Health Concerns in Celiac Disease

verification.note: Immunogenicity demonstrated in dietary/celiac context; direct relevance to a crosslinked surgical implant is inferred, not directly demonstrated.

question: Q3
claim: Single-amino-acid substitutions in mTG recognition tag sequences can modulate immunogenicity while retaining transglutaminase reactivity.
evidence: Review of mTG bioengineering notes that specific single-residue substitutions in tag sequences strongly modulate potential immunogenicity with retained reactivity, a lever for engineering safer variants.

sources.title: Bioengineering of microbial transglutaminase for biomedical applications

verification.note: Reported as a design principle in a review; specific low-immunogenicity clinical variant not yet demonstrated.

question: Q3
claim: Dual crosslinking of GelMA by UV photo-crosslinking plus mTG enzymatic crosslinking increases stiffness and reduces swelling versus either method alone without harming cell viability.
evidence: Photopatterned GelMA treated with mTGase showed improved stiffness and rheology, decreased swelling, and better preservation of patterned shapes compared to single UV or mTG crosslinking, with preserved viability.

sources.title: Dual Crosslinked Gelatin Methacryloyl Hydrogels for Photolithography and 3D Printing

verification.note: Demonstrated in vitro material improvement; not a sealant efficacy study.

question: Q3
claim: Microbial transglutaminase can enzymatically bond a photo-crosslinked GelMA implant to host tissue, improving adhesion of GelMA to human cartilage ex vivo.
evidence: mTG was used to effect bioadhesion of GelMA to host tissue, improving ex vivo adhesion of GelMA hydrogels to human cartilage, illustrating orthogonal photo-plus-enzymatic bonding.

sources.title: Microbial Transglutaminase Improves ex vivo Adhesion of Gelatin Methacryloyl Hydrogels to Human Cartilage (Frontiers)
Microbial Transglutaminase Improves ex vivo Adhesion of Gelatin Methacryloyl Hydrogels to Human Cartilage (PMC)

verification.note: Demonstrated ex vivo adhesion improvement on human tissue.

question: Q3
claim: Orthogonal bienzymatic systems combine mTG-crosslinked gelatin with HRP/tyramine-crosslinked hyaluronic acid to form interpenetrating-network hydrogels with tunable mechanics.
evidence: An IPN uses mTG to crosslink gelatin and horseradish peroxidase to crosslink tyramine-grafted hyaluronic acid, combining two independent enzymatic chemistries under mild conditions.

sources.title: Bienzymatically crosslinked gelatin/hyaluronic acid interpenetrating network hydrogels: preparation and characterization

verification.note: Demonstrated orthogonal dual-enzyme crosslinking in vitro.

question: Q3
claim: Adding a small Z-Gln-Gly transglutaminase substrate to gelatin lets mTG generate mechanically tough, conductive gelatin hydrogels.
evidence: Gelatin crosslinked with mTG using Z-Gln-Gly yielded mechanically tough and conductive hydrogels, expanding the property window achievable with enzymatic crosslinking.

sources.title: Mechanically Tough and Conductive Hydrogels Based on Gelatin and Z-Gln-Gly Generated by Microbial Transglutaminase

verification.note: Demonstrated in vitro mechanical/conductivity enhancement.

question: Q3
claim: Enzyme-only crosslinked natural-polymer hydrogels are biocompatible but often mechanically weak, which is the core rationale for combining mTG with a second (photo or peroxidase) crosslink.
evidence: Reviews note enzymatically crosslinked natural hydrogels have excellent biocompatibility and mild reactions but typically lack mechanical strength, addressed by dual crosslinking.

sources.title: Bienzymatically crosslinked gelatin/hyaluronic acid interpenetrating network hydrogels
Dual Crosslinked Gelatin Methacryloyl Hydrogels for Photolithography and 3D Printing

verification.note: Well-supported motivation; general finding.

question: Q3
claim: Coagulation Factor XIIIa is itself a transglutaminase that stabilizes clots by forming isopeptide crosslinks between fibrin alpha- and gamma-chains, increasing resistance to mechanical and proteolytic challenge.
evidence: FXIIIa crosslinks fibrin alpha/gamma chains, producing thinner, denser fibers, smaller pores, higher clot stiffness, and greater fibrinolysis resistance.

sources.title: Understanding blood clot mechanical stability: the role of factor XIIIa-mediated fibrin crosslinking in rupture resistance

verification.note: Well-established biology; establishes the biomimetic target for mTG-based designs.

question: Q3
claim: The gelatin-mTG sealant is explicitly biomimetic: its gel-forming mechanism mimics the final crosslinking stage of blood coagulation but uses non-blood proteins and a calcium-independent enzyme.
evidence: The gelatin/mTG adhesive replaces fibrinogen with gelatin and FXIIIa with calcium-independent mTG, reproducing the covalent-crosslinking step of clotting without plasma-derived components.

sources.title: Biomimetic sealant based on gelatin and microbial transglutaminase: an initial in vivo investigation

verification.note: Design rationale demonstrated and validated in vivo.

question: Q3
claim: Synthetic FXIIIa-mimetic strategies (e.g. PolySTAT) demonstrate that mimicking transglutaminase clot stabilization improves hemostasis, validating the biomimetic concept beyond mTG.
evidence: PolySTAT, an engineered fibrin-crosslinking polymer that mimics FXIII function, integrated into fibrin fibers and produced fortified clots resistant to enzymatic degradation, improving survival in a rat hemorrhage model.

sources.title: A Synthetic Fibrin-Crosslinking Polymer for Modulating Clot Properties and Inducing Hemostasis

verification.note: Demonstrated for a synthetic mimetic; mTG-specific clot-mimicry benefit is analogous, not identical.

question: Q3
claim: Gelatin-mTG (gelzyme) achieves rapid hemostasis in vivo, reaching complete hemostasis in about 2.5 minutes in rat liver and bleeding femoral artery models.
evidence: In rat liver wound and briskly bleeding femoral artery models the gelatin-mTG adhesive achieved complete hemostasis in ~2.5 minutes with substantial adhesive and cohesive strength.

sources.title: Biomimetic sealant based on gelatin and microbial transglutaminase: an initial in vivo investigation

verification.note: Demonstrated in rodent models; not human clinical data.

question: Q3
claim: A gelatin/transglutaminase/thrombin sealant significantly shortened time to hemostasis versus control in a dog liver-trauma model.
evidence: Mean time to hemostasis was 1.20 +/- 0.33 min in the gelatin-TG-thrombin group versus 6.70 +/- 0.64 min in controls in dog liver trauma, indicating strong performance for parenchymal bleeding.

sources.title: A novel hemostatic sealant composed of gelatin, transglutaminase and thrombin effectively controls liver trauma-induced bleeding in dogs

verification.note: Demonstrated in a large-animal model; adds thrombin, so not mTG alone.

question: Q3
claim: Gelatin-mTG gels reach clinically meaningful burst-pressure sealing, restraining ~200 mmHg in porcine skin burst tests.
evidence: In vitro burst-pressure tests with porcine skin showed gelatin-mTG gels form within ~30 minutes under moist conditions and restrain pressures up to 200 mmHg, above arterial pressure.

sources.title: Biomimetic sealant based on gelatin and microbial transglutaminase: an initial in vivo investigation

verification.note: Demonstrated in vitro; long gel time under some conditions is a limitation for acute bleeding.

question: Q3
claim: mTG crosslinking increases gelatin gel stiffness and slows degradation, positioning gelatin-mTG for resorbable/temporary sealing rather than permanent structural repair.
evidence: mTG crosslinking tunes gelatin mechanical properties and reduces swelling/degradation rate; gelatin remains bioresorbable, making it best suited to topical, resorbable, temporary hemostasis and sealing indications.

sources.title: Tunable physical and mechanical properties of gelatin hydrogel after transglutaminase crosslinking on two gelatin types
Improved Thrombin Hemostat Using the Cross-Linked Gelatin by Microbial Transglutaminase

verification.note: Property tuning demonstrated; the resorbable/temporary positioning is an inference from those properties.

question: Q3
claim: No mTG-gelatin surgical sealant is documented as FDA-approved, whereas competing PEG-based (DuraSeal, CoSeal) and fibrin sealants are approved, indicating a translation/regulatory gap.
evidence: FDA-approved surgical sealants identified are PEG-based (DuraSeal approved 2005, CoSeal) and fibrin sealants; gelatin-mTG appears only in preclinical literature and patents, not on approved-device lists.

sources.title: DuraSeal Dural Sealant System - FDA PMA summary
Gelatin-transglutaminase hemostatic dressings and sealants (US Patent 9,655,988)

verification.note: Absence-of-approval is inferred from approved-device lists; patents show active commercial interest but not clearance.

question: Q3
claim: Microbial transglutaminase is already produced industrially at scale by Streptomyces mobaraensis fermentation from low-cost substrates.
evidence: mTG is manufactured mainly via S. mobaraensis fermentation, enabling large-quantity production from inexpensive substrates, unlike scarce animal-tissue-derived transglutaminase.

sources.title: Whole-Genome Shotgun Assembly and Analysis of the Genome of Streptomyces mobaraensis DSM 40847, a Strain for Industrial Production of Microbial Transglutaminase

verification.note: Well-established: mTG is a commodity food-industry enzyme.

question: Q3
claim: mTG is calcium-independent, thermostable, and has broad substrate specificity, giving it processing and cost advantages over calcium-dependent mammalian transglutaminases.
evidence: Streptomyces-origin transglutaminase does not require calcium ions and acts on broadly diverse, small-molecular-weight acyl donors, indicating low cost and wide industrial applicability.

sources.title: Streptomyces mobaraensis - an overview (ScienceDirect Topics)

verification.note: Established biochemical advantage.

question: Q3
claim: Fermentation titers of mTG can be substantially raised by strain engineering and mutagenesis, improving cost efficiency.
evidence: A UV-mutagenized S. mobaraensis reached 37.51 U/mL (2.15x wild-type) in flask fermentation, and Corynebacterium ammoniagenes secreted ~2.5 g/L pro-transglutaminase in a jar fermentor; ARTP mutagenesis further boosts output.

sources.title: Enhancing transglutaminase production of Streptomyces mobaraensis by iterative mutagenesis breeding with ARTP
Secretion of Streptomyces mobaraensis pro-transglutaminase by coryneform bacteria

verification.note: Demonstrated titer improvements across strains/methods.

question: Q3
claim: Blood-derived fibrin sealants are constrained by cost and limited pathogen-screened plasma supply, a structural disadvantage that fermentation-based gelatin-mTG could avoid.
evidence: Plasma-derived fibrin sealants have limited applications because of cost and limited pathogen-screened plasma supply, with US clinical demand exceeding cryoprecipitation harvest capacity, driving interest in non-plasma alternatives.

sources.title: A totally recombinant human fibrin sealant

verification.note: Fibrin supply/cost constraint is documented; mTG advantage over it is a reasonable inference.

question: Q3
claim: Fibrin sealant unit prices span roughly under $50 to over $750 per product, giving a low-cost fermentation-derived gelatin-mTG a plausible cost-competitiveness target.
evidence: Reported fibrin sealant prices range from under $50 to over $750 depending on product; a commodity fermentation enzyme plus gelatin is intrinsically cheaper on raw-material cost.

sources.title: Costs Analysis of Fibrin Sealant for Prevention of Anastomotic Leakage in Lower Colorectal Surgery

verification.note: Fibrin price range documented; actual medical-grade gelatin-mTG cost-of-goods and pricing not published, so competitiveness is speculative.
